item.content:encoded:
The AHRC North-Sea Heritage in Transitions (NHT) is a major doctoral research initiative led by the University of Aberdeen, designed to develop research talent and strengthen the role of art history, visual arts, heritage and creative practice in Scotland’s North Sea region.

Supported through an Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) Doctoral Focal Award, the initiative brings together the University of Aberdeen, Robert Gordon University (RGU), and the University of the Highlands and Islands (UHI) to create a collaborative research environment focused on a region experiencing profound economic, environmental and cultural change.

The programme is particularly relevant to researchers interested in the relationship between heritage, visual culture, creative practice, environmental transition, industrial change, community development and cultural regeneration.

About the AHRC North-Sea Heritage in Transitions Initiative

The North-Sea Heritage in Transitions (NHT) initiative is an ambitious investment in doctoral research and research talent across Scotland’s North Sea region.

The initiative has been established to address the changing role of art, heritage, visual culture and creative practice within a region undergoing substantial economic, environmental and cultural transformation.

Rather than treating heritage simply as something connected to the past, NHT approaches heritage as an active and evolving part of contemporary regional life.

The initiative recognises that Scotland’s North Sea region is experiencing major changes in how communities, industries and landscapes are understood and represented. These changes create important questions for researchers working across the arts and humanities.

Through doctoral research, NHT aims to investigate these questions while developing researchers who can contribute to Scotland’s cultural sector and the wider national and international creative economy.

Why Is North-Sea Heritage in Transitions Important?

Scotland’s North Sea region has a distinctive history shaped by energy production, maritime exchange, industrial development and economic transformation.

For generations, the region has been closely associated with energy production and maritime activity. However, the transition toward a low-carbon future is changing the economic and social landscape.

This transition creates new challenges and opportunities for communities, cultural organisations, researchers, artists and heritage professionals.

The NHT initiative therefore asks important questions about how places and communities can understand, preserve, reinterpret and create heritage during periods of significant change.

The initiative focuses particularly on how art history, visual arts and creative practice can contribute to understanding and responding to these transformations.

Researching a Region in Economic Transition

The North Sea region is undergoing significant economic restructuring as traditional energy systems evolve and new low-carbon industries emerge.

Economic transition can affect much more than employment and industry. It can also influence:

  • Community identity
  • Local histories
  • Industrial heritage
  • Cultural institutions
  • Landscapes and built environments
  • Relationships between communities and places
  • Artistic practices
  • Regional narratives
  • Public perceptions of the future
  • Cultural and creative industries

NHT provides an opportunity for doctoral researchers to examine these interconnected issues through research in the arts and humanities.

The initiative recognises that cultural research can play an important role in helping communities understand where they have come from while considering what their future might look like.

Focus Areas of the NHT Research

The North-Sea Heritage in Transitions initiative centres on several interconnected areas of research.

1. Art History

Art history provides an important framework for understanding how people, places, communities and historical events have been represented over time.

Doctoral research within the NHT environment can contribute to understanding the visual history of the North Sea region and how artistic representations have changed alongside economic, environmental and social developments.

Research in this area may help explore questions concerning:

  • Historical representations of North Sea communities
  • Industrial and maritime imagery
  • Regional artistic traditions
  • Changing representations of landscapes
  • Cultural memory
  • Relationships between art and place
  • The interpretation of historical visual materials

2. Visual Arts

Visual arts are another central component of North-Sea Heritage in Transitions.

Visual practices can provide powerful ways of documenting and interpreting changes taking place within communities and landscapes.

As the region experiences economic and environmental transition, artists and researchers can explore how these changes are represented, remembered and experienced.

The initiative’s emphasis on visual culture creates space for research examining the relationship between visual representation, identity, place and transition.

3. Creative Practice

NHT also places significant emphasis on creative practice.

Creative practice can provide alternative approaches to research, allowing researchers and cultural practitioners to explore complex questions through artistic and experimental methods.

This can include approaches that connect research with:

  • Communities
  • Cultural organisations
  • Artists
  • Heritage practitioners
  • Digital technologies
  • Public engagement
  • Regional development
  • Environmental questions

The initiative therefore positions creative practice not only as a cultural activity but also as a means of research, engagement and regional development.

Heritage and Cultural Regeneration

One of the central ideas behind North-Sea Heritage in Transitions is that heritage and culture can contribute to regional regeneration.

As economic structures change, communities may need to reconsider how their histories and cultural identities are understood.

Heritage can contribute to this process by helping communities:

  • Preserve important histories
  • Understand changing landscapes
  • Maintain cultural identity
  • Reinterpret industrial legacies
  • Connect generations
  • Encourage community participation
  • Develop new cultural initiatives
  • Strengthen local creative economies

The initiative therefore connects doctoral research with broader questions about the future of Scotland’s North Sea region.

A Collaborative Doctoral Research Environment

A major feature of North-Sea Heritage in Transitions is its collaborative structure.

The initiative brings together three institutions:

University of Aberdeen

The University of Aberdeen leads the AHRC Doctoral Focal Award and provides a major research environment for the initiative.

Robert Gordon University

Robert Gordon University is a partner institution contributing to the collaborative doctoral research environment.

University of the Highlands and Islands

The University of the Highlands and Islands is also part of the partnership, helping extend the initiative’s research and regional connections.

This collaboration allows doctoral researchers to benefit from an environment that connects different academic perspectives, institutions and regional networks.

Building a New Generation of Researchers

NHT is designed not only to conduct research but also to develop research talent.

The initiative aims to establish distinctive doctoral cohorts capable of examining North Sea visual culture while working collaboratively with cultural practitioners.

This means that doctoral researchers can become part of a broader research community rather than working entirely in isolation.

The cohort-based approach can encourage:

  • Interdisciplinary collaboration
  • Peer learning
  • Research networking
  • Knowledge exchange
  • Engagement with cultural practitioners
  • Development of professional skills
  • Collaboration across institutions

For researchers planning careers in academia, cultural organisations, heritage, creative industries or related sectors, this type of research environment can provide valuable professional development.

Strengthening Creative and Digital Skills

Another major objective of NHT is to strengthen creative and digital capabilities.

The contemporary cultural sector increasingly requires researchers and practitioners who can combine traditional humanities knowledge with digital and creative skills.

Through its emphasis on art history, visual arts and creative practice, the initiative aims to enhance capabilities that can be relevant at:

  • Regional level
  • National level
  • International level

Digital skills can be particularly valuable for researchers working with contemporary visual culture, digital heritage, creative technologies and new forms of public engagement.

Partnerships and Career Development

North-Sea Heritage in Transitions also places strong emphasis on partnerships.

The initiative seeks to support partnerships that deliver North Sea-specific expertise while creating stronger career pathways in the arts, heritage and creative sectors.

This is important because doctoral graduates increasingly pursue careers beyond traditional academic positions.

Potential professional environments associated with the broader research and cultural ecosystem can include:

  • Universities and research institutions
  • Museums and galleries
  • Heritage organisations
  • Cultural policy organisations
  • Creative industries
  • Arts organisations
  • Digital cultural projects
  • Community-based cultural initiatives
  • Regional development organisations

The combination of doctoral research, creative skills and partnership experience can therefore help researchers develop expertise applicable across multiple professional environments.

Key Objectives of North-Sea Heritage in Transitions

The initiative’s work can be understood through three major objectives.

1. Develop distinctive doctoral cohorts

NHT aims to build doctoral research communities capable of analysing and creating North Sea visual culture.

Researchers will be encouraged to engage with cultural practitioners and address questions associated with:

  • Geopolitical change
  • Environmental transition
  • Social transformation
  • Cultural identity
  • Regional development

2. Strengthen creative and digital capabilities

The programme seeks to enhance creative and digital skills that can strengthen the capacity of researchers and practitioners across Scotland and beyond.

These skills are increasingly important within the modern arts, heritage and creative economy.

3. Create stronger partnerships and career pathways

NHT aims to establish partnerships that generate specialised knowledge about the North Sea region while supporting professional opportunities in the arts, heritage and creative sectors.

Why This Research Matters for the Future of the North Sea Region

The transition to a low-carbon economy is not simply a technological or economic process.

It also involves questions of identity, history, memory, community and culture.

When major industries change, communities may experience changes to employment, landscapes, institutions and collective identities.

Industrial and maritime heritage can become particularly important during these periods because it provides a connection between the region’s past and its emerging future.

Artistic and creative practices can help communities explore these changes in ways that complement conventional economic or environmental research.

This makes the NHT initiative particularly significant for researchers interested in the intersection between culture and transition.

Geographic and Regional Focus

The central geographical focus is Scotland’s North Sea region.

The initiative is concerned with the distinctive cultural, economic, environmental and historical characteristics of this region.

Its place-based approach means that research is expected to engage meaningfully with the region’s particular circumstances rather than treating cultural transition as an abstract or purely theoretical issue.

The North Sea region’s history of:

  • Energy production
  • Maritime exchange
  • Industrial transformation
  • Community development
  • Environmental change

provides a rich context for doctoral research.

Is There an Application Deadline?

No application deadline is provided in the information supplied for this opportunity.

The material describes the AHRC North-Sea Heritage in Transitions initiative and its research objectives but does not provide:

  • An application opening date
  • A closing date
  • A specific doctoral project deadline
  • A scholarship application deadline
  • An admissions deadline

Prospective applicants should therefore verify the current application timetable, available doctoral projects and funding conditions with the participating universities before making plans.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Important Information About Funding

The information provided identifies NHT as an AHRC Doctoral Focal Award, but it does not specify the individual funding amount, stipend, tuition-fee coverage, eligibility requirements or number of doctoral positions available.

Therefore, applicants should not assume that every doctoral position associated with the initiative has identical funding conditions.

Specific information such as:

  • Tuition fee coverage
  • Living stipend
  • Research expenses
  • International student eligibility
  • Residency requirements
  • Duration of funding
  • Application procedure
  • Individual research project requirements

should be checked against the official doctoral opportunity or project announcement.

Conclusion

The AHRC North-Sea Heritage in Transitions initiative represents an important investment in doctoral research at the intersection of art history, visual arts, creative practice and regional cultural transformation.

Led by the University of Aberdeen in partnership with Robert Gordon University and the University of the Highlands and Islands, the initiative responds to the profound changes taking place across Scotland’s North Sea region as the area moves from its historic dependence on energy production and industrial activity toward a lower-carbon future.

Its significance extends beyond academic research. By connecting doctoral researchers with cultural practitioners, creative organisations and regional partners, NHT aims to strengthen the cultural workforce, develop creative and digital capabilities, support community wellbeing and contribute to cultural regeneration.

For prospective researchers interested in heritage, visual culture, art history, creative practice and the cultural dimensions of economic and environmental transition, North-Sea Heritage in Transitions offers a distinctive research environment focused on one of Scotland’s most rapidly changing regions.

The initiative’s combination of doctoral training, interdisciplinary research, creative practice, regional engagement and cultural-sector partnerships makes it a potentially valuable pathway for researchers seeking to contribute to the future of arts, heritage and creative economies in Scotland and beyond.

Click HERE for more award opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
The Stanley 1913 Creators Fund 2027 is now open, offering $50,000 in funding to selected early-stage nonprofit organizations working to create stronger communities and develop innovative solutions to social challenges.

Stanley 1913 describes its community as Creators, Builders and Inventors who are committed to creating a better way of life and a better world. The Creators Fund builds on that philosophy by supporting emerging nonprofit leaders with bold ideas and the potential to create meaningful community impact.

Since 2023, the fund has supported 23 nonprofits across eight countries, covering a wide range of causes, communities and approaches to creating change.

About the Stanley 1913 Creators Fund

The fund is designed to provide early-stage nonprofits with financial support to help turn innovative ideas into action. Rather than focusing on one specific sector, the program supports organizations working across different causes and community challenges.

Successful organizations can receive $50,000, which can provide valuable resources for developing programs, strengthening operations, reaching communities and expanding the impact of an emerging nonprofit.

The fund is particularly relevant to organizations that are:

  • Developing innovative solutions to community challenges
  • Led by emerging nonprofit leaders
  • In the early stages of their development
  • Creating measurable social or community impact
  • Building new approaches to solving important problems

What Makes a Strong Applicant?

Applicants should be able to clearly explain the problem their organization is addressing and how their solution is creating positive change.

A strong application should demonstrate:

  • A clear problem: What challenge is the organization addressing?
  • An innovative solution: What is the organization doing differently?
  • Community impact: Who benefits from the work?
  • Potential for growth: How could the organization expand its impact?
  • Use of funding: How would $50,000 help move the organization’s work forward?

The fund’s emphasis on “Creators, Builders and Inventors” means applicants should demonstrate more than a good idea. They should show how they are turning that idea into meaningful action.

Funding and Benefits

Selected nonprofits can receive:

  • $50,000 in funding
  • Recognition as part of the Stanley 1913 Creators community
  • An opportunity to strengthen their nonprofit’s work
  • Resources to develop or expand innovative community solutions
  • Greater visibility for their organization’s mission and impact

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is aimed at early-stage nonprofit organizations and emerging nonprofit leaders working on innovative solutions that can strengthen communities.

The fund is not presented as being limited to one particular cause, race or ethnic group. Stanley 1913 states that previous recipients have represented different causes, people and approaches to creating change.

The supplied announcement does not provide a complete list of eligible countries for the 2027 cycle. Applicants should therefore check the official application guidelines to confirm geographic and organizational eligibility.

APPLY HERE

Deadline

The 2027 application announcement does not specify a closing date.

Applicants should check the official Stanley 1913 Creators Fund application page for the current deadline and application requirements.

How to Apply

Interested organizations should review the official 2027 application requirements and submit their application through the designated Stanley 1913 Creators Fund application process.

Applicants should ensure that they clearly communicate their organization’s mission, the problem they are solving, their innovative approach, community impact and how the funding would help advance their work.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Stanley 1913 Creators Fund 2027

Opportunity Category

Grant

Target Applicants

Early-stage nonprofit organizations and emerging nonprofit leaders developing innovative solutions to strengthen communities.

Conclusion

The Stanley 1913 Creators Fund 2027 offers an opportunity for emerging nonprofits to secure $50,000 in funding to develop innovative solutions and increase their community impact.

With previous support reaching 23 nonprofits across eight countries, the fund provides an opportunity for emerging organizations to gain financial resources while advancing ideas aimed at creating a better world.

For more global grants, scholarships, fellowships, internships, jobs, conferences, competitions, and other career opportunities for young people, visit the Opportunities for Youth (OFY) website at www.opportunitiesforyouth.org.

item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of State Paid Student Internship Program for Spring 2027 and Summer 2027 offers eligible students, recent graduates, and U.S. military veterans an opportunity to gain substantive professional experience while contributing to the formulation and implementation of U.S. foreign policy.

The program provides interns with exposure to the work of the U.S. Department of State, including its domestic offices, diplomatic facilities, and overseas posts. Selected interns can potentially work on assignments involving international affairs, diplomacy, economic research, public affairs, visa and citizen services, international conferences, policy-related work, administration, information systems, and other areas connected to the Department’s mission.

Importantly, the internship is paid, with the announcement listing compensation of $19.96 per hour at the GS-04 level. The internship is full-time and requires participants to work 40 hours per week for 10 consecutive weeks.

Opportunity Overview

  • Opportunity: U.S. Department of State Paid Student Internship Program
  • Intake: Spring 2027 and Summer 2027
  • Host organization: U.S. Department of State
  • Location: Department of State posts in the United States and overseas
  • Duration: 10 consecutive weeks
  • Work schedule: Full-time, 40 hours per week
  • Pay: $19.96 per hour
  • Grade: GS-04
  • Security clearance: Secret
  • Application period: August 7, 2026, to September 1, 2026
  • Deadline: September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time
  • Work arrangement: Not remote; telework is not available
  • Travel: Reasonable travel expenses to and from the required Washington, D.C. orientation and internship location are covered
  • Announcement number: INT-2026-0002
  • Control number: 879740200

What Is the U.S. Department of State Student Internship Program?

The U.S. Department of State Student Internship Program is designed to give students and eligible veterans meaningful exposure to U.S. foreign policy and the operations of the Department of State.

Rather than being limited to observation or basic office duties, the program provides educational and professionally substantive experiences. Depending on the office or overseas assignment, interns may become involved in projects and responsibilities that expose them to diplomacy, international relations, public service, foreign policy, economic affairs, communications, administration, and other areas.

The Department notes that former interns have undertaken a wide variety of assignments, including contributing to congressionally mandated reports, participating in negotiations, supporting U.S. citizen services and visa-related work, coordinating international conferences and visits by senior officials, conducting economic research, monitoring media reporting, and identifying experts for overseas engagements.

Students with scientific and technical backgrounds may also find assignments related to areas such as arms control, infectious diseases, and remote sensing. Those interested in management and administration may contribute to projects involving budgets, human resources, information systems, and logistical support for overseas posts.

This breadth makes the program relevant to students pursuing careers not only in diplomacy and international affairs, but also in communications, economics, public administration, technology, science, management, and related fields.

What Will Interns Do?

The exact responsibilities depend on the domestic office or overseas post to which an intern is assigned.

The Department of State explains that duties can vary significantly according to the assignment. Examples of work previously undertaken by interns include:

  • Contributing to congressionally mandated reports.
  • Participating in negotiations.
  • Supporting U.S. citizen services.
  • Assisting with visa-related work.
  • Helping coordinate international conferences.
  • Supporting visits involving high-level officials.
  • Conducting economic research.
  • Monitoring and evaluating media reporting.
  • Identifying U.S. experts for overseas speaking engagements.
  • Working on scientific and technical issues.
  • Supporting projects involving arms control.
  • Contributing to work related to infectious diseases.
  • Working on remote sensing issues.
  • Supporting budgets and financial-related projects.
  • Assisting with human resources activities.
  • Working with information systems.
  • Providing general logistical support to overseas posts.
  • Performing certain routine administrative responsibilities where required.

This means applicants should not assume that every internship placement will have the same responsibilities. The nature of the assignment will depend on the bureau, office, geographical location, and functional area selected.

Spring 2027 Internship

Applicants interested in the Spring 2027 intake should take note of the following timeline:

  • Application period: August 7 to September 1, 2026
  • Selection committee review: September 7, 2026
  • Selection/non-selection and tentative offer notification: Mid-September 2026
  • Information gathered for security-clearance initiation: September 18, 2026
  • eQIP initiation: September 22, 2026
  • Seasonal security-clearance deadline: December 15, 2026
  • Internship season: January 19 to May 28, 2027

The actual start date is contingent upon successful completion of the required security-clearance process.

Summer 2027 Internship

Applicants who prefer the Summer 2027 intake will follow a similar application process but a different selection and onboarding schedule.

The timeline is:

  • Application period: August 7 to September 1, 2026
  • Selection committee review: September 18, 2026
  • Selection/non-selection and tentative offer notification: October 9, 2026
  • Information gathered for security-clearance initiation: October 23, 2026
  • eQIP initiation: October 30, 2026
  • Seasonal security-clearance deadline: March 12, 2027
  • Internship season: May 17 to August 27, 2027

Again, the internship start date depends on successful completion of the security-clearance requirements.

Financial Benefits and Compensation

One of the most attractive features of this opportunity is that it is a paid federal internship.

The vacancy announcement lists a salary of:

$19.96 per hour

The position is classified at:

GS-04

Interns are required to work full-time, 40 hours per week, for a period of 10 consecutive weeks.

In addition to the hourly compensation, the program provides reasonable travel expenses associated with traveling to and from the mandatory orientation in Washington, D.C., as well as travel to and from the internship location.

The program therefore provides participants with both paid professional experience and exposure to the work of a major U.S. government institution.

Mandatory Washington, D.C. Orientation

Successful interns are required to attend a standard-setting mandatory orientation in Washington, D.C.

Completion of this orientation is required for successful participation in the internship. The program covers reasonable travel expenses associated with traveling to and from the orientation and internship location.

Applicants should therefore consider this requirement before applying, particularly if they are selected for an assignment outside Washington, D.C.

Who Can Apply?

This is an important part of the opportunity because the program has specific citizenship and eligibility restrictions.

The announcement states that the opportunity is open to U.S. citizens, including eligible U.S. undergraduate students, graduate students, recent graduates, and U.S. military veterans with a strong interest in the Department of State.

Applicants must meet the core conditions below.

1. U.S. Citizenship

Applicants must be U.S. citizens at the time of application.

This means the opportunity is not generally open to international students who are citizens of other countries.

2. Minimum Age

Applicants must be at least 18 years old at the time of application.

3. Security Clearance

Applicants must be able to receive and maintain a Secret security clearance.

This is an important requirement because the internship involves work within the U.S. Department of State and potentially sensitive government activities.

4. Previous Participation

Applicants must not have previously participated in the:

  • U.S. Department of State Student Internship Program;
  • U.S. Foreign Service Internship; or
  • Foreign Service Fellowship Program.

5. Medical Insurance

Applicants must be able to provide proof of medical insurance for the duration of the internship.

Coverage must also apply during travel to and from the internship location, including international insurance coverage where an overseas placement is involved. Applicants are responsible for their personal medical and health-related expenses during the internship.

Four Eligibility Pathways

Applicants must qualify through at least one of four eligibility pathways.

Option 1: Current Undergraduate Students

Current undergraduate students can qualify if they:

  • Are enrolled in an accredited two-year or four-year college or community college.
  • Have completed at least 60 credit hours by the start of the internship.
  • Are enrolled at least part-time when applying, although breaks in enrollment of up to five months are permitted.
  • Are in good academic standing.
  • Have a minimum 3.2 GPA.

This pathway is particularly relevant to undergraduate students who have already completed a substantial portion of their degree and want to gain practical experience in foreign policy and public service.

Option 2: Current Graduate Students

Current graduate students can qualify if they:

  • Are enrolled in a graduate program at an accredited institution.
  • Are enrolled at least part-time when applying, subject to the permitted breaks in enrollment.
  • Are in good academic standing.
  • Have a minimum 3.2 GPA.

Graduate students in fields connected to international affairs, diplomacy, political science, economics, communications, public policy, international development, security studies, science, technology, management, and related disciplines may find the program particularly relevant, although the announcement does not restrict eligibility to a specific academic major.

Option 3: Recent Graduates

Recent graduates can qualify if they:

  • Graduated from an accredited undergraduate or graduate program within two years of the internship start date.
  • Earned a minimum 3.2 GPA.

This provides an opportunity for eligible recent graduates who have completed their studies but are still within the specified two-year eligibility period.

Option 4: U.S. Military Veterans

U.S. military veterans can qualify if they:

  • Are veterans of the United States Armed Forces.
  • Possess a high school diploma or equivalent.
  • Served on active duty for any length of time within the two years preceding the internship start date.

What Skills and Backgrounds Could Be Relevant?

Because internship assignments vary across Department of State offices and posts, the program can accommodate a broad range of academic and professional interests.

Potentially relevant areas include:

  • International relations
  • Diplomacy
  • Foreign policy
  • Political science
  • International development
  • Economics
  • Communications
  • Journalism and media
  • Public affairs
  • Public administration
  • Management
  • Human resources
  • Information systems
  • Science and technology
  • Security studies
  • International security
  • Research
  • Policy analysis
  • Conference coordination
  • Administrative support
  • Logistics

The announcement specifically describes previous intern assignments involving policy, negotiations, citizen services, visas, international conferences, economic research, media monitoring, scientific and technical subjects, budgets, human resources, information systems, and logistics.

Applicants should nevertheless ensure that their application demonstrates how their own education, experience, skills, interests, and career objectives connect with the internship.

Security Clearance: An Important Part of the Application

A major consideration for applicants is the required Secret security clearance.

The Department of State explains that routine Secret-level clearances normally take approximately 120 to 150 days, although investigations can take substantially longer in certain circumstances.

The process may take longer where an applicant has circumstances such as:

  • Extensive overseas travel;
  • Overseas education;
  • Overseas residence;
  • Overseas employment;
  • Dual citizenship;
  • Foreign contacts;
  • Immediate family members who are foreign citizens;
  • Relatives who are foreign citizens; or
  • A spouse or partner who is a citizen of another country.

The Department also notes that security, suitability, or medical issues can affect the processing timeline. These circumstances do not necessarily mean that an applicant will be denied clearance, but they may make the process longer.

The Department further explains that, because the period between conditional selection and entry on duty may only be two to four months, it may not always be possible to complete a non-routine investigation before the scheduled internship begins.

Applicants interested in overseas placements should therefore pay particular attention to the security-clearance requirements and potential implications of foreign ties.

What Documents Are Required?

Applicants must submit the required application materials for their application to be considered complete.

The required documents include:

  1. Resume
  2. Current or most recent transcript

Both official and unofficial transcripts are accepted during the application process. However, selected candidates may subsequently be required to provide an official transcript before beginning the internship.

Applicants should therefore make sure their transcript clearly demonstrates the academic eligibility requirements applicable to their chosen pathway.

For example, undergraduate and graduate applicants should ensure that their academic record supports the required 3.2 GPA threshold.

How the Application Process Works

The application process consists of several stages.

Part I: Applicant Profile

Applicants who are new to USAJOBS must create an applicant profile and provide the required biographical and prior federal government employment information.

Applicants who already have a USAJOBS profile can proceed to the internship application.

The announcement states that applicants do not need to build a separate USAJOBS resume if they have already attached a personal resume to their profile.

Part II: Internship Application

The second part is specifically focused on the Department of State Student Internship Program.

Applicants will be required to answer questions concerning their:

  • Personal experience;
  • Academic experience;
  • Employment experience;
  • Internship preferences; and
  • Statements of interest.

Applicants must also identify whether they prefer Spring 2027 or Summer 2027 and indicate whether they are interested in domestic and/or overseas assignments.

Part III: Required Documents

Applicants must attach:

  • Their resume; and
  • Their official or unofficial transcript.

The announcement emphasizes that applications submitted before the deadline without the required documents will not be considered.

Choosing a Geographical or Functional Area

Applicants can identify up to two geographical or functional areas for which they wish to be considered.

Those seeking overseas assignments must first identify the bureau responsible for the location.

For example, an applicant interested in an assignment at a U.S. Embassy in La Paz, Bolivia, would select the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs, according to the example provided in the announcement.

This makes it important for applicants to think carefully about the type of work and geographical environment in which they would like to gain experience.

Statements of Interest Are Extremely Important

One of the most important elements of the application is the Statements of Interest.

The Department explicitly describes these statements as a critical part of the selection process.

Applicants are expected to make their statements:

  • Clear;
  • Concise;
  • Well written;
  • Professionally presented;
  • Relevant to the internship;
  • Focused on their objectives and motivation.

The statements should demonstrate effective communication and commitment to advancing U.S. national interests through public service.

Applicants should explain how their:

  • Academic studies;
  • Professional experience;
  • Personal responsibilities;
  • Skills;
  • Technical expertise;
  • Language abilities; and
  • Other relevant experiences

have prepared them for the internship.

The Department encourages applicants to demonstrate qualities such as:

  • Professionalism;
  • Integrity;
  • Accountability;
  • Sound judgment;
  • Resilience;
  • Adaptability;
  • Problem-solving;
  • Commitment to public service; and
  • Ability to contribute effectively to mission-driven teams.

Applicants should also explain what they would contribute to the office or post and what they hope to gain from the internship.

How Applicants Are Evaluated

Applications are evaluated based on merit.

Department officials consider factors including:

  • Education;
  • Work experience;
  • Volunteer experience;
  • Training;
  • Overall background;
  • Experience demonstrated in the application; and
  • Responses to applicant questions.

The Department may make final selections based on a review of application materials alone or through a phone interview.

This means applicants should not assume that an interview will necessarily be part of the process. Their written application must therefore be strong enough to communicate their qualifications, motivation, and suitability for the program.

Is the Internship Remote?

No.

The vacancy announcement states:

  • Telework eligible: No
  • Remote job: No

The opportunity involves physical placement at Department of State posts, either domestically or overseas depending on the assignment.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to participate in person for the duration of the internship.

Is Relocation or Travel Supported?

Yes, the program states that reasonable travel expenses to and from the internship are reimbursed.

This is particularly relevant for interns assigned away from their current location.

The program also covers reasonable travel expenses associated with the required Washington, D.C. orientation.

However, applicants should carefully review the official offer and program instructions to understand the precise scope of covered expenses.

Internship Duration

The Department of State Student Internship Program requires participants to serve for 10 consecutive weeks.

The Spring 2027 internship season runs from January 19 through May 28, 2027, while the Summer 2027 internship season runs from May 17 through August 27, 2027.

Participants must work 40 hours per week to successfully complete the internship.

Why This Internship Is Valuable for Future Careers

The U.S. Department of State is responsible for significant aspects of U.S. diplomacy and international engagement. An internship within the Department can therefore provide exposure to how a major government institution approaches foreign policy, international relations, diplomacy, public service, and global issues.

Depending on the assignment, interns may gain experience in areas such as:

1. International Affairs

Interns can gain practical exposure to international issues and the work of government officials involved in U.S. foreign policy.

2. Diplomacy and Negotiations

Previous interns have participated in negotiations and other activities connected with international diplomacy.

3. International Conferences and High-Level Visits

Interns may assist with international conferences and visits involving senior officials, providing valuable experience in event coordination and diplomatic engagement.

4. Communications and Media

Some assignments involve monitoring and evaluating media reporting, making the program potentially relevant to students interested in public affairs, communications, journalism, and strategic communications.

5. Economic Research

Applicants interested in economics, international development, trade, finance, or economic diplomacy may benefit from assignments involving economic research.

6. Public Administration

Students interested in government administration can potentially work on budgets, human resources, information systems, and logistics.

7. Science and Technology

The Department also describes opportunities involving scientific and technical subjects, including areas such as infectious diseases, arms control, and remote sensing.

Race, Nationality, and Geographic Eligibility

The opportunity should not be interpreted as a globally open internship.

The key eligibility requirement is U.S. citizenship.

The announcement states that applicants must be U.S. citizens at the time of application. It also identifies U.S. citizens, nationals, or those who owe allegiance to the United States as part of the relevant USAJOBS hiring pathway.

The announcement also states that federal hiring decisions are based on merit, qualifications, and the needs of the service and are made without regard to non-merit factors such as race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to a particular racial group or ethnic background. However, non-U.S. citizens generally do not meet the stated citizenship requirement.

Important Deadline

The application period for both the Spring 2027 and Summer 2027 intakes is:

August 7, 2026, to September 1, 2026

The application must be completed by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on September 1, 2026, including submission of the required documents.

Applicants are encouraged to submit their applications well before the deadline rather than waiting until the final day.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted electronically through the Gateway to State application system via the official USAJOBS vacancy.

The application process requires applicants to:

  1. Create or access their USAJOBS applicant profile.
  2. Complete the Department of State Student Internship application.
  3. Select their preferred internship season.
  4. Indicate their domestic and/or overseas assignment preferences.
  5. Select up to two geographical or functional areas.
  6. Complete the required applicant questions.
  7. Prepare clear and compelling Statements of Interest.
  8. Upload their resume.
  9. Upload their current or most recent transcript.
  10. Submit the complete application before the deadline.

Official application: U.S. Department of State Paid Student Internship Program on USAJOBS

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

Although meeting the minimum eligibility requirements is essential, applicants should also focus on presenting a strong and coherent application.

Make Your Resume Relevant

Rather than simply listing every activity you have undertaken, emphasize experiences that demonstrate:

  • Research ability;
  • Writing and communication;
  • Leadership;
  • Teamwork;
  • International or cross-cultural exposure;
  • Analytical skills;
  • Problem-solving;
  • Public service;
  • Project management;
  • Technical skills;
  • Foreign-language abilities;
  • Volunteer service; and
  • Relevant academic achievements.

Demonstrate Your Motivation

The Department specifically emphasizes the importance of Statements of Interest.

Applicants should clearly explain why they want to work with the Department of State and how the internship fits into their professional development and long-term goals.

Connect Your Education to the Assignment

Do not simply state your degree title.

Explain how your academic training has equipped you with knowledge or skills that can contribute to the work of a Department office or overseas post.

Highlight Relevant Experience

Experience does not necessarily have to come from a government position.

Professional employment, volunteer service, research, student leadership, military service, community work, internships, and other substantive activities can demonstrate valuable competencies.

Demonstrate What You Can Contribute

Applicants should answer an important question:

What will the Department of State gain by selecting you?

The application should show the practical skills, knowledge, perspectives, language abilities, technical expertise, work ethic, and professional qualities the applicant would bring to the assignment.

APPLY HERE

Key Things Applicants Should Not Overlook

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should carefully verify the following:

  • You are a U.S. citizen.
  • You are at least 18 years old.
  • You meet one of the four eligibility pathways.
  • You meet the applicable 3.2 GPA requirement where required.
  • You have the necessary academic credits if applying as an undergraduate.
  • You have not previously participated in the specified Department of State internship or fellowship programs.
  • You can obtain and maintain the required Secret security clearance.
  • You have appropriate medical insurance.
  • Your resume is attached.
  • Your transcript is attached.
  • Your Statements of Interest are complete and professionally written.
  • You have selected Spring 2027 or Summer 2027.
  • You have considered your domestic and/or overseas assignment preferences.
  • You have selected up to two geographical or functional areas.
  • You can work 40 hours per week for 10 consecutive weeks.
  • You are prepared to attend the mandatory Washington, D.C. orientation.
  • You submit the entire application before September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Visit HERE for more information about the U.S. Department of State Paid Student Internship Program 2027.

Final Thoughts

The U.S. Department of State Paid Student Internship Program for Spring 2027 and Summer 2027 is a significant professional development opportunity for eligible U.S. citizen students, recent graduates, and military veterans interested in foreign policy, diplomacy, international affairs, public service, communications, economics, administration, science, technology, and related areas.

What makes the program particularly valuable is its combination of paid employment, substantive professional responsibilities, exposure to U.S. foreign policy, potential domestic and overseas assignments, and experience within the U.S. Department of State.

Selected interns may contribute to real-world activities involving negotiations, international conferences, economic research, media monitoring, citizen services, visa work, scientific issues, administrative operations, and other Department functions.

However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to the program’s eligibility restrictions. U.S. citizenship is mandatory; applicants must be at least 18 years old, and candidates must be able to obtain a Secret security clearance. The academic pathways also include specific requirements relating to enrollment, credit hours, graduation dates, and GPA.

The deadline for both the Spring 2027 and Summer 2027 cohorts is September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Because the application requires a resume, transcript, detailed questions, and carefully prepared Statements of Interest, eligible candidates should begin preparing their applications early rather than waiting until the final hours.

For eligible candidates seeking to build a career in diplomacy, foreign policy, international affairs, public administration, communications, or other areas connected to U.S. government service, this internship can provide an important foundation for future professional opportunities.

The Danish Diabetes and Endocrine Academy (DDEA) is inviting applications for eight 2/3-financed PhD scholarships for candidates interested in advancing research in diabetes, metabolism, and endocrinology.

Each scholarship is worth DKK 1,100,000, covering salary and tuition fees for two years of a three-year PhD period. This provides an excellent opportunity for researchers to pursue doctoral studies at a Danish university while contributing to cutting-edge research in these fields.

Funding Benefits

Successful applicants will receive a 2/3-financed PhD scholarship valued at DKK 1,100,000.

The funding covers:

  • Salary for two years of the three-year PhD period
  • Tuition fees for the funded period
  • Support for pursuing research at a Danish university

The scholarship allows successful candidates to develop their research while working within Denmark’s academic and scientific environment.

Research Areas

Applications are welcome for research projects in any field within:

  • Diabetes
  • Metabolism
  • Endocrinology

Applicants should propose research that demonstrates strong academic quality and potential to contribute to knowledge within their chosen field.

Eligibility Requirements

To apply for the DDEA PhD Scholarship, candidates must meet the programme requirements.

Applicants must:

  • Hold a Master’s degree from a Danish university or an equivalent degree from a foreign university approved by the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science.
  • Be applying as a PhD candidate, rather than as a Principal Investigator.
  • Not already be enrolled as a PhD student at the time the grant notification is issued on November 26, 2026.
  • Have a principal supervisor employed at the faculty of the Danish university where the applicant intends to enrol.
  • Have a principal supervisor who conducts research as an associate professor or professor within the relevant subject area.

If an applicant has not yet completed their Master’s examination, they must provide a statement from their Master’s thesis supervisor confirming when the thesis will be submitted and when the examination will take place.

The Master’s degree certificate must subsequently be submitted to the DDEA Secretariat no later than six months after receiving the grant notification.

Important Application Conditions

Applicants may submit an application for only one PhD scholarship per application round across the different DDEA PhD scholarship calls.

Applicants should also communicate with their prospective principal supervisor before applying. A principal investigator can host only one 2/3 DDEA-funded PhD scholar or one two-year DDEA-funded postdoctoral fellow at a time, subject to the conditions specified by DDEA.

Candidates are therefore encouraged to confirm their eligibility and supervisory arrangements before submitting an application.

Application Procedure

Interested candidates should:

  1. Identify a suitable research area within diabetes, metabolism, or endocrinology.
  2. Identify a Danish university and an eligible principal supervisor.
  3. Develop a strong PhD research proposal.
  4. Confirm that they meet the DDEA eligibility requirements.
  5. Prepare the required supporting documents.
  6. Submit the application through the official DDEA application system before the deadline.

Applicants should carefully review the official guidelines and funding terms before submitting their application.

Evaluation and Selection

The scholarships are awarded through a competitive selection process.

Applications are assessed according to DDEA’s established evaluation criteria and guidelines. Candidates should therefore ensure that their proposed research demonstrates strong academic quality, relevance to the eligible research areas, and a clear research plan.

The expected date for notification of the grant decision is November 26, 2026.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply is:

August 18, 2026, at 23:59 CET

Applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their applications well before the deadline to allow sufficient time to coordinate with their proposed supervisor and complete all required materials.

How to Apply

Applications and the full programme guidelines are available through the official Danish Diabetes and Endocrine Academy website.

Read the full guidelines and apply here

Conclusion

The DDEA PhD Scholarships 2026 provide a valuable opportunity for aspiring researchers to pursue doctoral research in diabetes, metabolism, and endocrinology at a Danish university. With eight scholarships available and funding of DKK 1,100,000 per award, the programme can provide significant financial support during two years of a three-year PhD programme.

If your academic interests align with the eligible research areas and you meet the Master’s degree, enrolment, and supervision requirements, this is an opportunity worth considering. Start preparing your research proposal and connect with a potential principal supervisor early, then submit your complete application before August 18, 2026.
